courseTitle: Ionic - Build iOS, Android & Web Apps with Ionic & Angular

cues.en: Now if you know Angular, you know how you can handle forms there
and here I want to use the template-driven approach,
so in Angular, we would simply wrap our form with the form element, with the normal HTML form element.
So for example here, we could wrap this entire grid which contains our form inputs and the buttons that
belong to the form with a form element.
Now let me close that here
and this is how Angular would by default
as long as we add our forms module here which is added by default to imports in the module that contains
the page or the component we place the form on, as long as we have that forms module from Angular forms,
Angular will automatically detect this form element and setup a form object behind the scenes for us
where it then allows us to register inputs and then it manages these inputs automatically.
Now how does that work in Ionic?
Just like that. It is a web app in the end,
never forget this,
it's a web app where we use Angular and therefore, we can use all these default Angular features without
any changes.
So by wrapping our form inputs here and the buttons with a form tag and making sure that we do import
forms module in the module that holds the auth page,
we get this template-driven approach to work out of the box, without any additional configuration needed.
Now the only confusing thing might be, well but we're not using normal inputs and buttons,
we're using ion-inputs and ion-buttons.
The thing is these web components just wrap these normal inputs in buttons and they are written by the
Ionic team in a way such that they expose all the APIs, all the different features normal inputs do.
So an ion-input can be used just like a normal input in an Ionic form,
you don't need any special configuration,
instead you can simply add ngModel on there and the name attribute which you need to add when working
with the template-driven approach and give this any name you want,
like e-mail and you're good, Angular can now detect this input and add it to the form which is automatically
created for you.
You can of course also add validation as you know it,
so for the template-driven approach, you add validation by adding directives on the input,
for example here, we could add the required directive and the e-mail directive to make it clear that this
input is both required and should be an e-mail and therefore of course I'll set the type here from text to
e-mail which will make sure that we also get the right keyboard to open up on a real device,
so the right soft keyboard which automatically gives us simple access to the @ sign and so on.
So with that, I configured the first input,
now we can also configure the second input and there again, I add ngModel and a name and the name
here can be password
but you're free to choose any name and I will require that
and we can also add the minlength directive here which both the ion-input supports out of the box
as well as Angular. Angular supports the minlength directive and it will automatically validate whatever
we enter here to have a minimum length of whatever value we enter here.
So let's say our password should be at least six characters long,
well then we just have to add minlength six here.
When I say Ionic also supports this, you'll see in a second what I mean by that and why this is
pretty amazing.
So we have our two inputs configured,
we have our form, Angular should now be able to automatically detect all of that but in order to get
access to that form, we need to add a local reference on that form element which can have any name you
want, like f or form,
I'll just go with f and you actually assign a value to that and the value here has to be ngForm.
What this does is it gives you access to this form object Angular created for you and it gives you access
to this form object by giving you a reference to it stored in that f local reference.
So now everywhere in this template, we can get access to that form through that f local reference and therefore
for example here, we can add an ngSubmit event listener here and call onSubmit there and here, I forward
f, so this local reference and this allows me to then accept the form Angular created for us in the onSubmit
method and in case you're wondering, ngSubmit is a special directive Angular gives us that
will prevent the default which would be that the form submission actually sends a request to the back-end
which we don't want and instead it just captures the event that gives us access to all the form
data.
So now we just have to add an onSubmit method and we have to make sure that this form gets submitted only
by that login button and I do make sure that this is the case by giving this a type of submit and giving
the other button a type of button.
So the first button will now not submit the form, only the second button will. Let's now add the onSubmit
method in the auth.page.ts file and there, we will get a form which is of type ngForm and
ngForm is a type
you need to import from @angular/forms
and let's simply for now console log this form object to see what's inside of it
and now let's see what that gives us.
Let's wait for this page to reload,
here's our form
and if I press login,
you see I get this ngForm thing here, under controls,
you see a list of all the controls Angular registered for us and
that is the e-mail and password control because these are the two inputs on which we added ngModel and
we also have that value field which is a Javascript object with our control names, e-mail and password,
so the names we assigned on these ion-inputs in our template and the value which was in them when the
form was submitted.
So this works but it's not just the submission that works. If we go back and for example I tap in here
and I leave that, you now see I have a red border.
So we automatically get some error styles here out of the box and that's the case because if we inspect
this, this ion-item here actually receives some classes like ion-invalid, ion-touched
and that's again the ion-item working together with the ion-input.
As I mentioned before, the ion-input has these Angular classes like ngInvalid, ngPristine
and so on, it also has these Ionic-specific classes and that is what I meant with Ionic also understands
minlength and so on. Ionic also has these basic validation features built into its components,
its input components and therefore it is also able to correctly show you error styles and it also has
some extra adjustments for the Angular package. So it's able to show you error styles when your validation
error is out here and therefore we got these nice error styles out of the box without us needing to do anything.
